tip: ‘cei di’ is the future of ‘cael’, meaning you will get. So ‘cei di ddirwy’ means you'll get a fine, not one you already got.
‘i'w gwblhau’ means to complete it. The ‘'w’ packs it in before the verb, so the noun isn't repeated.
After ‘o’ (of), the next word softens: ‘cariad’ becomes ‘gariad’, giving ‘symbol o gariad’.
‘a’ (and) changes the start of the next verb: ‘prynu’ becomes ‘phrynu’. ‘aeth Owain... a phrynu’ = went and bought.
‘cael’ + ‘eu’ + a verb says something is done to it: ‘cael eu gwnïo’ = are sewn. ‘eu’ points back to ‘gwisgoedd’, the costumes.
‘roeddwn i'n’ + a verb sets the background; a short past-tense verb cuts in: ‘darllen... pan aeth’ = reading when it went out.
‘hon’ means this for feminine nouns. ‘cymuned’ is feminine, so it's ‘i'r gymuned hon’. A masculine noun would take ‘hwn’.
‘mynd â’ means to take along: ‘es i â'r ci am dro’ = I took the dog for a walk, literally went with the dog.
‘heb i’ + a person means without them doing something: ‘heb iddo sylwi’ = without him noticing.
‘cyn i’ + a person softens the verb: ‘coginio’ becomes ‘goginio’. ‘cyn iddi goginio’ = before she cooked.
Welsh normally shows ‘of’ by word order, not a separate word: ‘llif yr afon’ = the flow of the river, literally flow the river, with ‘yr’ on the last noun.
The object after a past-tense verb softens its first word: ‘dysgu’ becomes ‘ddysgu’ after ‘dechreuais i’ (I started).
After ‘o’ (from), the sound softens ‘Ll’ to ‘L’: ‘Lloegr’ becomes ‘Loegr’ in ‘o Loegr’.
The ending ‘-ûm’ is a literary past ‘I’. ‘cyfarfûm i’ (I met) is more formal than spoken ‘cwrddais i’.
Adjectives normally follow the noun in Welsh: ‘cawl blasus’ is literally soup tasty, for tasty soup.
A verb-noun can be the subject, like the English -ing form: ‘parcio’ means parking in ‘mae parcio'n anodd’.
‘ga i...?’ asks may I and softens the next verb: ‘defnyddio’ becomes ‘ddefnyddio’.
‘mynd’ is irregular in the past: ‘est ti’ means you went, as in ‘est ti i'r parti’ (did you go to the party).
Putting the subject first with ‘wnaeth’ adds emphasis: ‘Owain wnaeth ffeindio’ means it was Owain who found.
After ‘rhaid i’ + a person, the verb softens: ‘cofio’ becomes ‘gofio’ in ‘rhaid i mi gofio’.
The ‘-wn i’ ending is the would form: ‘hoffwn i’ means I would like, gentler than saying I want.
The object me wraps the verb as ‘fy...i’: ‘fy helpu i’ means help me in ‘alli di fy helpu i’.
‘arfer’ after ‘roedd’ means used to, for past habits: ‘roedd hi'n arfer byw’ is she used to live.
You thank to someone in Welsh: ‘diolch’ takes ‘i’, so ‘diolchodd hi i'r meddyg’ is she thanked the doctor.
To her contracts to ‘iddi’, and the verb softens: ‘talu’ becomes ‘dalu’ in ‘rhaid iddi hi dalu’.
After ‘os’ (if), the present ‘doi di’ covers the future: ‘os doi di'n gynnar’ means if you come early.
‘roedd e'n gweithio’ (was working) is the ongoing background, and the ‘-ais’ past ‘ffoniais i’ marks the one-off event.
Indirect yes/no questions use ‘a’ for whether: ‘gofynnodd... a oeddwn i’ means asked if I was.
I should have is ‘dylwn i fod wedi’ + a verb: ‘dylwn i fod wedi edrych’ means I should have looked.
Need is felt on you in Welsh: ‘angen... arna i’ means I need, so ‘roedd angen... arna i’ is I needed.
